content: Microsoft Excel, officially known as Microsoft Office Excel, is a spreadsheet application developed and distributed by Microsoft for use on Microsoft Windows and Mac OS X platforms. It provides features such as calculation, graphing tools, pivot tables, and a macro programming language called Visual Basic for Applications (VBA), except in the case of Excel 2008 for Mac OS X, which lacks VBA support. Excel has been the dominant spreadsheet application for these platforms since version 5, released in 1993, and is included as part of the Microsoft Office suite. It is one of the most widely used microcomputer applications to date. History Microsoft initially marketed a spreadsheet program called Multiplan in 1982, which was popular on CP/M systems. However, it lost popularity to Lotus 1-2-3 on MS-DOS systems. Excel 2.0, designed to align with the Mac version and bundled with a runtime Windows environment, was released in November 1987. Lotus was slow to adapt 1-2-3 for Windows, and by 1988, Excel began outselling 1-2-3, helping Microsoft establish itself as a leading PC software developer. This achievement solidified Microsoft’s position as a competitor in the software industry and demonstrated its future in developing graphical user interface (GUI) software. Microsoft continued to release new versions of Excel approximately every two years. The current version for Windows is Excel 12, also known as Microsoft Office Excel 2007, while the current version for Mac OS X is Microsoft Excel 2008. Early in its development, Excel became the subject of a trademark lawsuit by another company that had already been selling a software package named Excel in the finance industry. As a result, Microsoft was required to refer to the program as Microsoft Excel in all formal press releases and legal documents. Over time, this practice was largely abandoned, and Microsoft resolved the issue permanently by purchasing the trademark from the other company. Microsoft also encouraged the use of the abbreviation XL as shorthand for the program. While this is no longer common, the program's icon on Windows still features a stylized combination of the letters X and L, and the default Excel file format uses the extension .xls. Excel introduced several user interface improvements over earlier electronic spreadsheets, while retaining the fundamental structure of rows and columns containing data or formulas, as seen in the original spreadsheet program, VisiCalc. Excel was the first spreadsheet to allow users to customize the appearance of spreadsheets, including fonts, character attributes, and cell formatting. It also introduced intelligent cell recomputation, where only cells dependent on the modified cell are updated, unlike earlier programs that recalculated everything or required a specific user command. Excel has extensive graphing capabilities and supports mail merge functionality. When Excel was first bundled into Microsoft Office in 1993, Microsoft Word and Microsoft PowerPoint had their GUIs redesigned for consistency with Excel, which was considered the killer app for PCs at the time. Since 1993, Excel has included VBA, a programming language based on Visual Basic, which allows users to automate tasks and create user-defined functions (UDFs) for use in worksheets. VBA is a powerful addition to Excel, featuring a fully integrated development environment (IDE) in later versions. Macro recording can generate VBA code that replicates user actions, enabling simple automation of repetitive tasks. VBA also allows the creation of forms and in-worksheet controls for user interaction. The language supports the use (but not creation) of ActiveX (COM) DLLs, and later versions include support for class modules, enabling basic object-oriented programming techniques. However, the automation functionality provided by VBA has made Excel a target for macro viruses, which became a significant issue in corporate environments until antivirus products began detecting these viruses. Microsoft eventually added features to disable macros entirely, enable them selectively, or trust only macros signed with a trusted certificate. File Formats Until the 2007 version, Microsoft Excel used a proprietary binary file format called Binary Interchange File Format (BIFF) as its primary format. Excel 2007 introduced Office Open XML as its primary file format, an XML-based container similar in design to the XML Spreadsheet (XMLSS) format first introduced in Excel 2002. However, the XMLSS format cannot encode VBA macros. While promoting the use of new XML-based formats, Excel 2007 remains backward compatible with traditional binary formats. Additionally, most versions of Excel can read legacy formats such as CSV, DBF, SYLK, and DIF. The binary format specification was previously available from Microsoft upon request, but since February 2008, the XLS format specification can be freely downloaded and implemented under the Open Specification Promise patent licensing. Programming A key feature of Excel is its ability to write code using the programming language VBA. This code is written in a separate editor and controls the manipulation of spreadsheet entries using objects. Functions or subroutines written in VBA can take input from the spreadsheet and instantly write results back to the spreadsheet or display them on charts. This makes the spreadsheet an interface or window to the code, enabling easy interaction with the calculations performed by the code. Criticism Excel has faced criticism for issues common to spreadsheets in general, as well as specific problems such as accuracy, date handling, and display errors in Excel 2007. Accuracy Excel's reliance on floating-point calculations has led to criticism of its statistical accuracy and the absence of certain statistical tools. Proponents argue that these errors represent edge cases and that the relatively few users affected are aware of them and have workarounds or alternatives. Date Problems Excel incorrectly assumes that the year 1900 is a leap year, a bug inherited from Lotus 1-2-3 for backward compatibility. This legacy issue persists in the Office Open XML file format. Excel also supports a second date format based on the 1904 epoch. Excel 2007 Display Error On September 22, 2007, it was reported that Excel 2007 displayed incorrect results in specific situations. For example, the product of 77.1 and 850 is 65,535, but Excel displayed 100,000 for this calculation. Adding or subtracting one from this result displayed correct values, but the original product was displayed incorrectly. This error was introduced with changes to Excel's display logic in the 2007 version and did not exist in earlier versions. Microsoft released a fix for this issue on October 9, 2007, and it was also corrected in Service Pack 1. A detailed explanation of the bug, its likely cause, and the hotfix was provided by Chris Lomont.
